summary: Wind, sand, and a dream of flight brought Wilbur and Orville Wright to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina where, after four years of scientific experimentation, they achieved the first successful airplane flights on December 17, 1903. With courage and perseverance, these self-taught engineers relied on teamwork and application of the scientific process. What they achieved changed our world forever.

image.caption: Busts and Moon
image.altText: Copper busts of the two brothers with the moon visible in the blue sky.

fees.title: Per person
fees.detail: Fee is charged per-person, NOT per vehicle. Ages 15 and younger are free of charge.

fees.title: Education/academic groups
fees.detail: Structured educational visits that serve a curriculum need for a class may apply for a waiver for entrance fees in advance.

visitorInfo.operatingHours: These are the times the park grounds and visitor center are open for visitors.
visitorInfo.directions: Wright Brothers National Memorial is located along US 158 in the town of Kill Devil Hills on the Outer Banks of North Carolina.
visitorInfo.weather: Weather on the Outer Banks varies seasonally and daily. Summers can be very hot and sunny (wear sunscreen and drink water), while winters can be cold and wet. High winds are always a possibility any time of the year. It is not uncommon for a brief winter snow each year. Being on a barrier island, the memorial is susceptible to storm impacts, including hurricanes in the summer and nor'easters in the winter. No matter what time of year you visit, dress for the weather, and be ready for wind!

name: Wupatki
summary: Nestled between the Painted Desert and ponderosa highlands of northern Arizona, Wupatki National Monument is an unlikely landscape for a thriving community. The early 1100's marked a time of cooler and wetter weather, when the ancestors of contemporary Pueblo communities created a bustling center of trade and culture. For indigenous peoples, these sites represent the footprints of their ancestors.

image.caption: Wupatki Pueblo
image.altText: a large stone pueblo in a desert beneath mostly sunny skies with mountains in background

fees.title: Private vehicle
fees.detail: This fee covers the occupants of one private vehicle for seven days at both Sunset Crater Volcano and Wupatki National Monuments.

fees.title: Motorcycle
fees.detail: Valid for 7 days. Admits up to 2 private, non-commercial motorcycles with up to 4 total passengers to both Sunset Crater Volcano and Wupatki National Monuments.

fees.title: Per person
fees.detail: This fee covers entry for one bicyclist or pedestrian for seven days at both Sunset Crater Volcano and Wupatki National Monuments.

fees.title: Education/academic groups
fees.detail: Educational groups visiting the monument for a curriculum related visit should apply for an Academic Fee Waiver. If no fee waiver is obtained, educational groups will be charged as non-commercial groups.

visitorInfo.operatingHours: The Wupatki National Monument Visitor Center is open 9:00AM to 4:30PM MST March 8th- November 1st. The visitor center is closed Tuesdays through Thursdays November 2nd- march 7th and is closed for December 25th and January 1st. Trails to Wupatki, Wukoki, Citadel, Nalakihu, Box Canyon, and Lomaki Pueblos are open daily from sunrise to sunset.
visitorInfo.directions: Wupatki and Sunset Crater Volcano National Monuments are connected by loop road FR-545 (paved). Visitors can enter the loop road near mile markers 430 (Sunset Crater Volcano) and 444 (Wupatki) on U.S. Highway 89.
visitorInfo.weather: Be prepared for variable and extreme weather conditions. You may expect high winds any time of year, summer temperatures above 100ºF (38ºC), afternoon thunderstorms July–September, and occasional snow in winter and early spring. Dress in layers, as Wupatki weather can change quickly at any time of year. For current weather please visit https://www.nps.gov/wupa/planyourvisit/weather.htm

name: World War II Memorial
summary: Through stone architecture and bronze sculptures, the World War II Memorial recognizes the ways Americans served, honors those who fell, and recognizes the victory they achieved to restore freedom and end tyranny around the globe.

image.caption: A Field of Stars
image.altText: Close up of Gold Stars in the Memorial

visitorInfo.operatingHours: The World War II Memorial is open 24 hours a day every day of the year. Restrooms, museums and elevators close in the evenings (check individual sites for hours). Park Rangers and volunteers are generally available between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m. to answer questions and provide assistance.
visitorInfo.directions: GPS Coordinates: 38.889413, -77.040553 Address: 1750 Independence Ave. SW, Washington, D.C. Nearest Intersection: 17th St. & Independence Ave. SW
visitorInfo.weather: Washington DC gets to see all four seasons. Humidity will make the temps feel hotter in summer and colder in winter. Spring (March - May) Temp: Average high is 65.5 degrees with a low of 46.5 degrees Summer (June - August) Temp: Average high is 86 degrees with a low of 68.5 degrees Fall (September - November) Temp: Average high is 68 degrees with a low of 51.5 degrees Winter (December - February) Temp: Average high is 45 degrees with a low of 30 degrees (Source: www.usclimatedata.com)

name: World War I Memorial
summary: A grateful nation honors the service, valor, courage and sacrifice of the 4.7 million American sons and daughters who served in the Great War.

image.caption: General Pershing Statue
image.altText: General Pershing Statue

visitorInfo.operatingHours: The WWI Memorial is open 24 hours a day.
visitorInfo.directions: 1493 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Nearest Intersection: 15th St NW and Pennsylvania Ave NW
visitorInfo.weather: Washington DC gets to see all four seasons. Humidity will make the temps feel hotter in summer and colder in winter. Spring (March - May) Temp: Average high is 65.5 degrees with a low of 46.5 degrees Summer (June - August) Temp: Average high is 86 degrees with a low of 68.5 degrees Fall (September - November) Temp: Average high is 68 degrees with a low of 51.5 degrees Winter (December - February) Temp: Average high is 45 degrees with a low of 30 degrees (Source: www.usclimatedata.com)

name: Yorktown Battlefield
designation: Part of Colonial National Historical Park
summary: Discover what it took for the United States to be independent as you explore the site of the last major battle of the Revolutionary War. Here at Yorktown, in the fall of 1781, General George Washington, with allied American and French forces, besieged General Charles Lord Cornwallis’s British army. On October 19, Cornwallis surrendered, effectively ending the war and ensuring independence.

image.caption: Cannon at Sunset Yorktown Battlefield
image.altText: Cannon at sunset at Yorktown Battlefield

fees.title: Per person
fees.detail: Adult (16 and older) -$15; good for 7 days entrance to Yorktown Battlefield (and NPS areas at Historic Jamestowne); can be upgraded to see Preservation Virginia areas at Historic Jamestowne for an additional $15 at the Historic Jamestowne Visitor Center. Yorktown Battlefield will not be selling the $30 entrance permit for Historic Jamestowne

visitorInfo.operatingHours: The Yorktown Battlefield Visitor Center and the Eastern National Store is open 9:00 am to 5:00PM Daily. . The Moore House, The Cemetery Lodge and the Poor Potter are closed but their grounds are open for visitation. The Nelson House is open as staffing permits. The Battlefield Tour Roads are open till Sunset.
visitorInfo.directions: For an internet map search or GPS, use the following: Yorktown Battlefield Visitor Center, 1000 Colonial Parkway, Yorktown, Virginia 23690. Eastbound from the Richmond area via I-64, exit 242B for Yorktown, to the Colonial Parkway. Follow the parkway to its end. West bound Interstate 64 from the Virginia Beach/Norfolk/Hampton area for Yorktown should take Route 105 East (Fort Eustis Boulevard east), exit 250B to Route 17. Turn left onto Route 17. Follow the signs to Yorktown Battlefield.
visitorInfo.weather: Yorktown, VA climate is warm during summer when temperatures tend to be in the 80's and cold during winter when temperatures tend to be in the 30's. The warmest month of the year is July with an average maximum temperature of 89.00 degrees Fahrenheit, while the coldest month of the year is January with an average minimum temperature of 28.10 degrees Fahrenheit. For closures in due to inclement weather at Colonial National Historical Park please phone this 24 hour phone number (757) 856-1240.

name: Yukon - Charley Rivers
summary: Located in Interior Alaska, Yukon-Charley Rivers offers exploration in a largely untouched landscape. Whether you float the mighty Yukon River or paddle the Charley River's whitewater, your memories will last a lifetime. Geology, cultural history, gold rush remnants, wildlife, and vast scenery will be a part of your experience. But, the strongest element will be solitude. Your adventure awaits.

image.caption: Aerial view of the Yukon River
image.altText: Aerial view of the Yukon River during fall colors

visitorInfo.operatingHours: The preserve is open 24-hours a day
visitorInfo.directions: Although there is no direct highway connection to Yukon-Charley Rivers National Preserve, visitors are able to access the preserve by either air travel from Fairbanks, or water or air travel from two small towns on the road system(Eagle and Circle), near the preserve boundaries.
visitorInfo.weather: The area that Yukon-Charley Rivers encompasses is generally classified as sub-arctic, with exceptionally cold winters, relatively warm summers, low annual precipitation, and generally high winds.

name: Yucca House
summary: Yucca House National Monument preserves a large unexcavated pueblo with a stunning setting in Montezuma Valley, nestled between Mesa Verde and Ute Mountain. Since Yucca House was protected as a national monument in 1919, it has remained largely untouched, offering intrepid visitors a sense of discovery and preserving the pueblo's beauty and integrity for future generations.

image.caption: Yucca House Spring
image.altText: Cattails with mesa in background.

fees.title: Entrance
fees.detail: There is no fee to enter Yucca House National Monument.

visitorInfo.operatingHours: Open year-round, weather pending. No services are available.
visitorInfo.directions: From Cortez, take Hwy. 491 south approximately 8 miles. Take a right on MC County Road B (green sign), which is a dirt road one mile south of MC Road C. Drive 0.8 miles, crossing a paved road (MC Road 21), and take the next dirt road on the right (before the farmhouse on the left). Follow this road north and west for 1.4 miles, and head towards a white ranch house with a red roof on the west horizon. Once at the ranch house, Yucca House NM is on the left side if the driveway.
visitorInfo.weather: Spring and Fall are mild with daytime temperatures ranging from 50 F to 80 F. Winter temperatures are below 50 F with occasional snowstorms. Summers are hot and dry, with highs in the 90s.

name: Anza-Borrego Desert
summary: California's largest state park: badlands, palm oases, slot canyons and wildflower springs in the Colorado Desert east of San Diego. Named for the explorer Juan Bautista de Anza and the borrego, the desert bighorn sheep.

image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Miskatonic assumed (based on copyright claims)., via Wikimedia Commons

name: Big Basin Redwoods
summary: California's oldest state park, in the Santa Cruz Mountains — a bowl of old-growth coast redwoods draining down Waddell Creek to the sea. Much of the forest burned in 2020 and is regrowing.

name: Julia Pfeiffer Burns
summary: A stretch of the Big Sur coast where McWay Falls drops 80 feet from a cliff onto a cove beach, with redwood canyons inland. Named for a pioneer rancher of Big Sur.

name: Humboldt Redwoods
summary: Home of Rockefeller Forest, the largest remaining old-growth coast redwood forest in the world, along the Eel River in northern California. The Avenue of the Giants runs through it.

name: Point Lobos
summary: A granite headland south of Carmel where cypress groves, coves and tide pools meet one of the richest marine habitats in California. Sea otters, seals and, in season, grey whales are often seen offshore.

name: Mount Tamalpais
summary: The 2,571-foot mountain rising above Marin County, with redwood canyons, oak woodland and views over San Francisco Bay from its summit. It surrounds Muir Woods National Monument.

image.credit: Oscar Vasquez / California Department of Parks and Recreation, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Emerald Bay
summary: One of Lake Tahoe's most photographed bays, with Fannette Island — the lake's only island — Eagle Falls, and Vikingsholm, a 38-room mansion in Scandinavian style on the shore.

name: Valley of Fire
summary: Nevada's oldest state park: red Aztec Sandstone that seems to burn in low sun, carved into arches, domes and narrow canyons, with petroglyphs left by ancient peoples. An hour northeast of Las Vegas.

name: Dead Horse Point
summary: A mesa-top overlook 2,000 feet above a gooseneck of the Colorado River, next to Canyonlands National Park near Moab. Known for sunrise views and dark night skies.

name: Goblin Valley
summary: A basin of thousands of mushroom-shaped hoodoos — the goblins — in the San Rafael Desert of central Utah, free to wander among on foot.

name: Snow Canyon
summary: A canyon of red and white Navajo Sandstone with lava flows, lava tubes and sand dunes, on the edge of St. George in southwestern Utah.

name: Kodachrome Basin
summary: Colourful sandstone and nearly 70 tall stone spires, or sand pipes, near Bryce Canyon in southern Utah, named after Kodachrome film by a National Geographic expedition.

name: Coral Pink Sand Dunes
summary: Shifting dunes of pink-orange sand below red cliffs in southern Utah, home to a beetle found nowhere else and popular for sandboarding and off-road driving.

name: Antelope Island
summary: The largest island in the Great Salt Lake, with bison, pronghorn and bighorn sheep, salt-flat beaches and huge flocks of migrating birds. Reached by a causeway from near Salt Lake City.

name: Custer
summary: South Dakota's first and largest state park, in the Black Hills: prairie and granite peaks, a large free-roaming bison herd, and the Needles Highway and Wildlife Loop Road.

name: Smith Rock
summary: Cliffs of volcanic tuff and basalt above a bend of the Crooked River in central Oregon, considered the birthplace of American sport climbing.

name: Silver Falls
summary: Oregon's largest state park, where the Trail of Ten Falls follows Silver Creek's canyon past ten waterfalls — four of which you can walk behind.

image.credit: Kelvin Kay -- Kkmd at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Deception Pass
summary: Forested islands, beaches and tidal currents around the narrow channel between Whidbey and Fidalgo Islands in Washington, spanned by the twin arches of the 1930s Deception Pass Bridge.

name: Palouse Falls
summary: A 200-foot waterfall plunging into a basalt canyon in southeast Washington's Channeled Scablands, carved by the ice-age Missoula Floods. Washington's official state waterfall.

image.credit: Bala Sivakumar from Seattle, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chugach
summary: Nearly half a million acres of mountains, glaciers and valleys right on the eastern edge of Anchorage, one of the largest state parks in the country.

name: Denali
summary: Mountains and lakes along the Parks Highway east of Denali National Park, with some of the best views of Denali from the road on clear days.

name: Kachemak Bay
summary: Alaska's first state park: glaciers, mountains, fjords and coastline across the bay from Homer, reached only by boat or plane.

image.credit: Beeblebrox ( talk ) 06:06, 13 January 2009 (UTC), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Nā Pali Coast
summary: Sheer, fluted sea cliffs and hanging valleys along Kauaʻi's northwest shore, reached on foot only by the Kalalau Trail, or seen from boats and the air. The valleys were farmed by Hawaiians for centuries.

name: Waimea Canyon
summary: The "Grand Canyon of the Pacific": a canyon about ten miles long and up to 3,000 feet deep on Kauaʻi, cut into red volcanic rock by rivers fed from one of the wettest places on Earth.

name: Kartchner Caverns
summary: A living limestone cave in southern Arizona, discovered by two cavers in 1974 and kept secret for years to protect it. Seen only on guided tours.

name: Slide Rock
summary: A natural water slide in the slippery bed of Oak Creek, among red rocks north of Sedona, Arizona, beside a historic apple farm.

image.credit: Don Graham from Redlands, CA, USA - God bless it!, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Roxborough
summary: Tilted slabs of red sandstone jutting from the foothills south of Denver — the same rock as Red Rocks and the Garden of the Gods. A National Natural Landmark.

image.credit: Greg Willis from Denver, CO, usa, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Eldorado Canyon
summary: A narrow canyon of sheer sandstone walls south of Boulder, Colorado, and one of the country's best-known climbing areas. Timed entry is needed on summer weekends.

name: Palo Duro Canyon
summary: The second-largest canyon in the United States, cut into the Texas Panhandle in banded red and gold rock. The outdoor musical TEXAS is staged in the canyon each summer.

image.credit: Larry D. Moore, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Big Bend Ranch
summary: The largest state park in Texas: remote desert mountains, canyons and the Rio Grande along the Mexican border, west of Big Bend National Park.

image.credit: Surfsupusa at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Enchanted Rock
summary: A huge dome of pink granite in the Texas Hill Country, rising about 425 feet above the land around it. The rock creaks as it cools at night, the source of many local legends.

name: Caprock Canyons
summary: Red-rock canyons on the edge of the Llano Estacado in the Texas Panhandle, home to the official Texas State Bison Herd.

name: City of Rocks
summary: Volcanic rock formations up to 40 feet high, rising from the high desert of southwestern New Mexico like the streets of a city.

name: Bruneau Dunes
summary: Home to the tallest single-structured sand dune in North America, beside small lakes in the desert of southwestern Idaho, with an observatory for dark-sky viewing.

name: Makoshika
summary: Montana's largest state park: badlands on the edge of Glendive with fossils of dinosaurs such as Triceratops and Tyrannosaurus in the Hell Creek Formation.

image.credit: Larry D. Moore, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hot Springs
summary: Hot springs in Thermopolis, Wyoming, that flow at 135°F over terraces of mineral deposits, with free bathing at the State Bath House and a state bison herd.

name: Itasca
summary: Minnesota's oldest state park, around Lake Itasca, where you can walk across the stones at the headwaters of the Mississippi River. Old-growth red and white pines grow along its shores.

image.credit: Mark Evans from Orange City, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Starved Rock
summary: Sandstone canyons with seasonal waterfalls along the Illinois River, Illinois's most visited state park, named for a legend of a siege on the butte above the river.

image.credit: Chris Light ( talk ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Devil's Lake
summary: Wisconsin's largest state park: a glacial lake ringed by 500-foot quartzite bluffs in the Baraboo Range, with boulder-field trails and rock climbing, northwest of Madison.

name: Porcupine Mountains Wilderness
summary: Old-growth hardwood forest, waterfalls and the Lake of the Clouds in the Porcupine Mountains along Lake Superior, in Michigan's Upper Peninsula — one of the largest old-growth forests west of the Adirondacks.

image.credit: w:Flickr user Erik Abderhalden, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tahquamenon Falls
summary: One of the largest waterfalls east of the Mississippi, where the root-beer-coloured Tahquamenon River drops over the Upper Falls in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, with a set of smaller Lower Falls downstream.

image.credit: Dawn Endico from Menlo Park, California, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hocking Hills
summary: Sandstone gorges, recess caves and waterfalls in southeastern Ohio, including Old Man's Cave, Ash Cave and Cedar Falls, linked by trails open all year.

name: Brown County
summary: Indiana's largest state park, in wooded hills near Nashville, known for its autumn colour and long views from its fire tower and overlooks.

name: Turkey Run
summary: Indiana's second state park: deep sandstone ravines along Sugar Creek, with ladders and narrow canyon trails, and a historic inn.

name: Cumberland Falls
summary: A 68-foot curtain of water on the Cumberland River in Kentucky, one of the few places in the Western Hemisphere where a moonbow forms regularly on clear nights at the full moon.

name: Fall Creek Falls
summary: Tennessee's largest state park, on the Cumberland Plateau, named for its 256-foot waterfall — among the highest free-falling falls in the eastern United States.

name: Cloudland Canyon
summary: A deep gorge cut into the western edge of Lookout Mountain in northwest Georgia, with rim views and two waterfalls at its foot.

image.credit: Ronmacal at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tallulah Gorge
summary: A 1,000-foot-deep gorge in northeast Georgia where the Tallulah River drops over a series of six waterfalls, with a suspension bridge across it and a floor reached by permit.

name: Providence Canyon
summary: Georgia's "Little Grand Canyon": gullies up to 150 feet deep, eroded since the 1800s from poor farming practices into soft sediments of pink, orange and purple.

name: Chimney Rock
summary: A granite spire rising above Hickory Nut Gorge near Asheville, North Carolina, with views over Lake Lure and a 404-foot waterfall nearby. Hurricane Helene in 2024 damaged the park and the village below it.

name: Jockey's Ridge
summary: The tallest active sand dune system in the eastern United States, on North Carolina's Outer Banks at Nags Head — a favourite for hang gliding and sunset walks.

image.credit: Pytheas at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Table Rock
summary: A granite mountain with a bare, flat-topped face at the edge of South Carolina's Blue Ridge, with a historic lodge and stonework built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Bahia Honda
summary: A Florida Keys island with some of the Keys' best beaches, clear water for snorkelling, and the remains of Henry Flagler's Overseas Railroad bridge.

name: John Pennekamp Coral Reef
summary: The first underwater park in the United States, off Key Largo in the Florida Keys, protecting coral reefs reached by snorkel and glass-bottom boat tours.

image.credit: Matt Kieffer from London, United Kingdom, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ichetucknee Springs
summary: Clear, spring-fed water flowing six miles through shaded forest in north Florida, famous for summer tubing and for swimming in its springs.

name: Myakka River
summary: One of Florida's oldest and largest state parks, with wetlands, prairies and a river full of alligators and wading birds, and a canopy walkway through the treetops.

name: Petit Jean
summary: Arkansas's first state park, on a mountain above the Arkansas River: Cedar Falls, a canyon, bluffs and lodge buildings built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Ha Ha Tonka
summary: The stone ruins of an early twentieth-century castle on a bluff above the Lake of the Ozarks in Missouri, with sinkholes, a natural bridge and a large spring.

image.credit: Paul Knittel from St. Louis, United States, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Letchworth
summary: The "Grand Canyon of the East": the Genesee River runs through a gorge up to 550 feet deep and over three large waterfalls in western New York.

name: Watkins Glen
summary: A narrow gorge in New York's Finger Lakes where a stone path and stairs lead past 19 waterfalls, under and behind some of them.

image.credit: Flickr user: Peter Rivera Stamford, Connecticut https://www.flickr.com/people/riverap1/, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Niagara Falls
summary: The oldest state park in the United States, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, on the American side of Niagara Falls with Goat Island, the American Falls and views of the Horseshoe Falls.

name: Ricketts Glen
summary: Old-growth forest and 24 named waterfalls along Kitchen Creek in northeastern Pennsylvania, many of them on the Falls Trail loop.

name: Ohiopyle
summary: Whitewater rafting and kayaking in the Youghiogheny River gorge of southwestern Pennsylvania, with waterfalls, natural water slides and the Great Allegheny Passage bike trail.

image.credit: Hubert Stoffels from Pittsburgh, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Baxter
summary: A wilderness park in north-central Maine around Katahdin, the state's highest mountain and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, given to the state by Governor Percival Baxter.

image.credit: TJ aka Teej at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Franconia Notch
summary: A mountain pass in New Hampshire's White Mountains with the Flume Gorge, the Cannon Mountain tramway and the site of the Old Man of the Mountain, which collapsed in 2003.

name: Mount Greylock
summary: The highest point in Massachusetts, crowned by a war memorial tower, and the state's first public land set aside to protect forest.

name: Cape Henlopen
summary: Dunes, beaches and maritime forest where Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, with Second World War observation towers and a fishing pier.

name: Blackwater Falls
summary: A 62-foot waterfall where the tea-coloured Blackwater River drops into its canyon in West Virginia's Allegheny Mountains, with a lodge on the rim.

image.credit: Tim Kiser ( w:User:Malepheasant ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grayson Highlands
summary: High balds, rocky outcrops and wild ponies on the slopes beside Mount Rogers in southwest Virginia, crossed by the Appalachian Trail.

image.credit: Virginia State Parks staff, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Natural Bridge
summary: A 215-foot-high limestone arch over Cedar Creek in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, the remains of an ancient cave roof, once owned by Thomas Jefferson.

name: Fort Robinson
summary: A former US Army fort in the Pine Ridge of northwest Nebraska, where the Lakota leader Crazy Horse was killed in 1877. Bison and bighorn sheep roam the buttes.

name: Maquoketa Caves
summary: More caves than any other state park in Iowa, with a natural bridge and limestone bluffs along a wooded valley, and buildings by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Robbers Cave
summary: Wooded hills and sandstone cliffs in the Sans Bois Mountains of southeast Oklahoma, with a cave said to have hidden outlaws including Belle Starr and Jesse James.

image.credit: Thomas & Dianne Jones from Okmulgee, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tishomingo
summary: Sandstone outcrops, a swinging bridge and canoe trips on Bear Creek in the Appalachian foothills of northeast Mississippi, on the Natchez Trace Parkway.

name: Gulf
summary: White-sand Gulf beaches, dunes, freshwater lakes and pine forest at Gulf Shores, Alabama, with a long fishing pier.

name: High Point
summary: The highest point in New Jersey, topped by a 220-foot war memorial obelisk, in the Kittatinny Mountains where New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania meet.

image.credit: AndyZ at en.wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grand Staircase-Escalante
summary: Vast, remote plateau and canyon country in southern Utah — the cliffs of the Grand Staircase, the Kaiparowits Plateau and the slot canyons of the Escalante — rich in dinosaur fossils. Its boundaries have been redrawn several times by presidential proclamation, most recently in 2026.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management (mypubliclands on Flickr) https://www.flickr.com/people/mypubliclands/, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Vermilion Cliffs
summary: Red cliffs, Paria Canyon and the swirling sandstone of Coyote Buttes, home of the Wave, on the Arizona–Utah line. Visiting the Wave needs a permit from a lottery, and California condors fly overhead.

name: Bears Ears
summary: Canyon country around a pair of buttes in southeastern Utah, with tens of thousands of cultural sites — cliff dwellings, rock art and granaries — sacred to the tribes who help manage it. Its boundaries have been redrawn by successive presidents.

name: Canyons of the Ancients
summary: The densest known concentration of archaeological sites in the United States, in southwestern Colorado: Ancestral Puebloan villages, towers and cliff dwellings, with the Anasazi Heritage Center as its museum.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks
summary: The jagged granite spires of the Organ Mountains above Las Cruces, New Mexico, and desert ranges to the west with petroglyphs and traces of the Butterfield stage route.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks
summary: Cone-shaped tent rocks of volcanic ash and pumice and a narrow slot canyon near Cochiti Pueblo, southwest of Santa Fe. The road crosses Pueblo land and the monument has been closed for long periods, so check before you go.

image.credit: VitaleBaby at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Carrizo Plain
summary: California's largest remaining native grassland, split by the San Andreas Fault, with the salt flats of Soda Lake, the rock art of Painted Rock and spring wildflower blooms.

image.credit: John Wiley User:Jw4nvc - Santa Barbara, California, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Basin and Range
summary: Remote, empty mountains and valleys in southeastern Nevada, with ancient rock art. Michael Heizer's vast land artwork City lies within it.

image.credit: U.S. Department of the Interior, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Gold Butte
summary: Red sandstone towers, rock art and desert tortoise habitat northeast of Las Vegas, with the remains of an old mining town, reached by rough roads.

image.credit: US Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Red Rock Canyon
summary: Red and cream sandstone cliffs 15 miles west of Las Vegas, with a 13-mile scenic drive, desert hiking and world-class climbing. The scenic drive needs a timed-entry reservation for much of the year.

name: Sonoran Desert
summary: Saguaro forests and desert mountain ranges southwest of Phoenix, crossed by historic trails used by Spanish explorers, the Mormon Battalion and the Butterfield stage.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Upper Missouri River Breaks
summary: Badlands, white sandstone cliffs and 149 miles of the Missouri River in central Montana, little changed since Lewis and Clark passed in 1805 — best seen by canoe.

name: Mojave Trails
summary: Desert mountains, lava flows, sand dunes and the longest undeveloped stretch of Route 66, between Interstates 15 and 40 in California's Mojave Desert.

image.credit: Bob Wick of the Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mount St. Helens
summary: The volcano that erupted on May 18, 1980, and the blast zone around it, left to recover naturally, with lava tubes at Ape Cave on its south side. Managed by the US Forest Service.

name: Newberry
summary: Lava flows, a glassy obsidian flow and two lakes in the caldera of the Newberry Volcano south of Bend, Oregon, with Lava Butte and the Lava River Cave. Managed by the US Forest Service.

image.credit: Q Myers, en:User:QDM, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Misty Fjords
summary: Sheer granite fjords, waterfalls and cliffs east of Ketchikan, Alaska, almost all of it wilderness and reached by boat or floatplane. Part of the Tongass National Forest.

image.credit: Zarxos at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Admiralty Island
summary: Kootznoowoo, the "fortress of the bears" in Tlingit: a big, forested island near Juneau with one of the densest brown bear populations in the world. Part of the Tongass National Forest.

image.credit: Nick Bonzey from Juneau, AK, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Arctic
summary: The largest wildlife refuge in the country, in Alaska's far northeast: Brooks Range peaks, tundra and the coastal plain where the Porcupine caribou herd gives birth. Gwich'in and Iñupiat homeland, with no roads in.

image.credit: Steven Chase, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bosque del Apache
summary: Wetlands along the Rio Grande in New Mexico where tens of thousands of sandhill cranes and snow geese spend the winter. Their flights at dawn and dusk draw crowds in November and December.

name: Okefenokee
summary: The largest blackwater swamp in North America, on the Georgia–Florida line: cypress, open prairies and floating peat islands, with alligators and sandhill cranes, explored by boat on water trails.

image.credit: US Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons

name: J.N. "Ding" Darling
summary: Mangrove estuary on Sanibel Island, Florida, known for wading birds such as roseate spoonbills and for its four-mile Wildlife Drive. Named for the conservationist cartoonist Jay Norwood "Ding" Darling.

name: Chincoteague
summary: Beaches, dunes and marsh on the Virginia end of Assateague Island, home of the Chincoteague ponies and a stop for huge numbers of migrating shorebirds and waterfowl.

image.credit: Leonard J. DeFrancisci, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Malheur
summary: Lakes and marshes in Oregon's high desert, one of the most important stopovers for migrating birds in the American West.

image.credit: Oregon Department of Transportation, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Wichita Mountains
summary: Granite mountains and mixed-grass prairie in southwest Oklahoma, the oldest managed refuge in the US Fish and Wildlife Service system. Bison were restored here in 1907, and elk and Texas longhorns roam too.

name: National Elk
summary: Winter range for one of the largest elk herds in North America, on the edge of Jackson, Wyoming. In winter, horse-drawn sleighs carry visitors among thousands of elk.

name: Chilkat
summary: Chilkat State Park is a 9,837-acre (3,980 ha) Alaska state park on a peninsula south of the town of Haines, Alaska between the Chilkat and Chilkoot inlets. Remote and known for the steep 14% grade gravel access road, the park offers campsites with minimal amenities and is open to fishing, hiking, boating, sea kayaking, and sightseeing. The campground is closed from October to mid-May due to winter concerns.

name: Chugach State Park Bluff Trail
managedBy: STATE OF ALASKA & SOUTH CENTRAL REGION & DIV OF LA

name: Fort Abercrombie
summary: Fort Abercrombie State Historical Park, also known as the Fort Abercrombie State Historic Site, is an Alaska state park on Kodiak Island, Alaska. It includes 182 acres (74 ha) of land at the end of Miller Point, located on the eastern shore of Kodiak Island northeast of the city of Kodiak. The park, established in 1969, is noted for its historical World War II fortifications and its scenery, which includes bluffs overlooking the ocean, spruce forests, and meadows.

name: Shuyak Island
summary: Shuyak Island State Park is an approximately 47,000 acre Alaska state park on most of Shuyak Island in the Kodiak Archipelago. The park includes a coastal forest of Sitka spruce, coastline, beaches, and waterways. The park contains four cabins for recreational use and is only accessible via air or water.

name: Totem Bight
summary: Totem Bight State Historical Park is a 33-acre (13 ha) state park in the U.S. state of Alaska. It is located north of Ketchikan.

image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bladon Springs
summary: Bladon Springs State Park is a public recreation area located on the site of four mineral springs that were once part of the historic spa at Bladon Springs, Choctaw County, Alabama. The park is operated in a partnership between Alabama State Parks and Choctaw County.

name: Blue Springs
managedBy: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
summary: Blue Springs State Park is a public recreation area located 7 mi (11 km) east of Clio in Blue Springs, Barbour County, Alabama. The 103-acre (42 ha) state park features a clear blue, natural underground spring that pumps 3,600 US gal (14,000 L) of water per minute into two concrete-ringed swimming pools. The park's recreational area was expanded in 2013 when the Forever Wild Land Trust purchased 100 acres (40 ha) adjoining acres for the purpose of providing hiking trails.

name: Buck's Pocket
summary: Buck's Pocket State Park is a public recreation area located on Sand Mountain in the northeast corner of the U.S. state of Alabama, two miles (3.2 km) north of the community of Grove Oak. The state park occupies 2,000 acres (810 ha) surrounding a natural pocket (canyon) of the Appalachian Mountain chain along South Sauty Creek, an upstream tributary on the east side of Guntersville Lake. The park is known for the sweeping views of its rugged, seemingly untouched landscape provided from the heights of Point Rock.

image.credit: Aaron Davis from Guntersville, AL, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cathedral Caverns
managedBy: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
summary: Cathedral Caverns State Park is a 493-acre (200 ha) public recreation area and natural history preserve in Kennamer Cove, Alabama, located approximately 5 miles (8.0 km) northeast of Grant and 7 miles (11 km) southeast of Woodville in Marshall County. The park, first known as Bats Cave , was developed as a tourist attraction in the 1950s. Cathedral Caverns was declared a National Natural Landmark in 1972 and opened as a state park in 2000.

name: Cheaha
summary: Cheaha State Park is a public recreation area located in Clay and Cleburne counties in Alabama, US. The park's 2,799 acres (1,133 ha) include Cheaha Mountain, the highest point in the state. The park adjoins Talladega National Forest and is managed by the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

name: Chewacla
summary: Chewacla State Park is a public recreation area occupying 696 acres (282 ha) below Interstate 85 on the far south side of Auburn, Alabama. The state park's central feature, 26-acre (11 ha) Lake Chewacla, provides opportunities for fishing, swimming, and non-motorized boating.

image.credit: Knizzle17 at en.wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chickasaw
summary: Chickasaw State Park is a 520-acre (210 ha) public recreation area located on U.S. Route 43 four miles (6.4 km) north of Linden in Marengo County, Alabama. The state park offers picnicking, playground, and minimal camping facilities and is a stop on the Alabama Black Belt Birding Trail.

name: DeSoto
managedBy: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
summary: DeSoto State Park is a public recreation area located on Lookout Mountain, eight miles (13 km) northeast of Fort Payne, Alabama. The state park covers 3,502 acres (1,417 ha) of forest, rivers, waterfalls, and mountain terrain. It borders the Little River, which flows into the nearby Little River Canyon National Preserve.

name: Desoto
summary: DeSoto State Park is a public recreation area located on Lookout Mountain, eight miles (13 km) northeast of Fort Payne, Alabama. The state park covers 3,502 acres (1,417 ha) of forest, rivers, waterfalls, and mountain terrain. It borders the Little River, which flows into the nearby Little River Canyon National Preserve.

name: Florala
summary: Florala City Park, formerly Florala State Park, is a 40-acre (16 ha) public recreation area in Florala, Alabama. The park wraps around the Alabama side of Lake Jackson, a 500-acre (200 ha) lake that straddles the Alabama-Florida state line.

name: Frank Jackson
summary: Frank Jackson State Park is a public recreation area that wraps around Lake Frank Jackson and forms the northwesternmost portion of the city of Opp, Alabama. The 2,050-acre (830 ha) state park offers facilities for fishing, boating, hiking, and camping.

name: J.P. Coleman
summary: J.P. Coleman State Park is a state park in the U.S. state of Mississippi. It is located ten miles (16 km) north of Iuka off Mississippi Highway 25, on the banks of the Tennessee River and Pickwick Lake.

name: Joe Wheeler
summary: Joe Wheeler State Park is a public recreation area with resort features located on Wheeler Lake, an impoundment of the Tennessee River, 18 miles (29 km) east of Florence in northwest Alabama. The state park contains 2,550 acres (1,030 ha) of land in three separate parcels and adjoins Wheeler Dam.

image.credit: Robert Nunnally from Allen, TX, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Guntersville
managedBy: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
summary: Lake Guntersville State Park is a public recreation area located on the far north side of the city of Guntersville in Marshall County, Alabama. The state park occupies 5,909 acres (2,391 ha) on the eastern shore of Guntersville Lake, a 69,000-acre (28,000 ha) impoundment of the Tennessee River. The park features resort facilities and is managed by the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

image.credit: benuski from Richmond, VA, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Lurleen
summary: Lake Lurleen State Park is a publicly owned recreation area located on U.S. Highway 82 approximately 9 miles (14 km) northwest of Northport in Tuscaloosa County, Alabama. The state park's 1,625 acres (658 ha) include 250-acre (100 ha) Lake Lurleen and a 23-mile (37 km) trail system.

name: Meaher
summary: Meaher State Park is a public recreation area located on Big Island, an island at the north end of Mobile Bay that lies within the city limits of Spanish Fort, Alabama. The state park occupies 1,327 acres (537 ha) along the shoreline of Ducker Bay, at the junction of Mobile Bay and the Mobile-Tensaw River Delta. It is surrounded by wetlands of the Mobile Bay estuary.

name: Monte Sano
managedBy: Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
summary: Monte Sano State Park is a public recreation area and mountaintop retreat encompassing 2,140 acres (870 ha) on the eastern portion of the top and slopes of Monte Sano Mountain on the east side of Huntsville, Alabama. The state park has 1930s-era, Civilian Conservation Corps–built rustic cottages, hiking trails and picnic areas with scenic overlooks, and modern campsites. It is managed by the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

name: Oak Mountain
summary: Oak Mountain State Park is a public recreation area located approximately 20 miles (32 km) south of Birmingham in the northeast quadrant of the city of Pelham, Alabama, United States. It is the state's largest state park at 9,940 acres (4,020 ha) and is home to the Alabama Wildlife Center, Oak Mountain Interpretive Center, and Oak Mountain BMX Track. Park activities include hiking, running, mountain biking, swimming, camping, fishing, horseback riding, and golf.

name: Paul M. Grist
summary: Paul M. Grist State Park is a public recreation area located 17 miles (27 km) north of Selma operated by the government of Dallas County, Alabama. The park offers water activities on a 100-acre (40 ha) lake as well as facilities for camping and picnicking.

name: Rickwood Caverns
summary: Rickwood Caverns State Park is a public recreation area and natural history preserve located 7 miles (11 km) north of Warrior, Alabama. The 380-acre (150 ha) state park offers tours of caverns with illuminated limestone formations estimated to be 260 million years old, blind cave fish, and an underground pool.

name: Roland Cooper
summary: Roland Cooper State Park is a public recreation area located six miles north of Camden, Alabama, on the eastern shore of Dannelly Reservoir, a 22,000-acre (8,900 ha) impoundment of the Alabama River known locally as the Millers Ferry Reservoir. The park features cottages, campground, fishing, and boating facilities.

name: Wind Creek
summary: Wind Creek State Park is a public recreation area located seven miles (11 km) south of Alexander City, Alabama, on the western side of Lake Martin, a 41,000-acre (17,000 ha) reservoir on the Tallapoosa River. The state park occupies 1,445 acres (585 ha) and is managed by the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

name: Bull Shoals White River
summary: Bull Shoals-White River State Park is a 732-acre (296 ha) Arkansas state park in Baxter and Marion Counties, Arkansas in the United States. Containing one of the nation's best trout-fishing streams, the park entered the system in 1955 after the United States Army Corps of Engineers built Bull Shoals Dam on the White River. The park runs along the shoreline of Bull Shoals Lake and the White River above and below the dam, and contains picnic areas, a marina, boat rentals, interpretive programs, and a visitors' center with gift shop.

image.credit: Flickr user: CoreBurn, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cane Creek
summary: Cane Creek State Park is a 2,053-acre (831 ha) Arkansas state park in Lincoln County, Arkansas in the United States. Straddling the Gulf Coastal Plain and the Mississippi Delta, the park includes the 1,675-acre (678 ha) Cane Creek Lake, a wooded lake which borders Bayou Bartholomew, the world's longest bayou. The park became a reality when the U.S.

name: Crowley's Ridge
summary: Crowley's Ridge State Park is a 291-acre (118 ha) Arkansas state park in Greene County, Arkansas in the United States atop Crowley's Ridge. Located on the former homesite of pioneer Benjamin Crowley, the park contains many excellent examples of the work done by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s. One of Arkansas's most popular state parks, the parks is bisected by Crowley's Ridge Parkway, a National Scenic Byway.

name: Daisy
summary: Daisy State Park is a 276-acre (112 ha) Arkansas state park in Pike County, Arkansas in the United States. The park at the foothills of the Ouachita Mountains features Lake Greeson, a 7,000-acre (2,800 ha) fishing lake constructed by the United States Army Corps of Engineers in 1950. The park is surrounded by timberlands and is located near the Ouachita National Forest.

image.credit: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Devil's Den
summary: Devil's Den State Park is a 2,200-acre (890 ha) Arkansas state park in Washington County, near West Fork, Arkansas in the United States. Park amenities were built by the Civilian Conservation Corps, beginning in 1933. Devil's Den State Park is in the Lee Creek Valley in the Boston Mountains, which are the southwestern part of The Ozarks.

name: Herman Davis
summary: Herman Davis State Park is a 1-acre (0.40 ha) state park in Manila, Arkansas, United States. The park includes the grave of and a memorial to Herman Davis (1888-1923), a U.S. sniper during World War I. The park is located at the junction of Baltimore Avenue and Arkansas Highway 18, south of the city center.

image.credit: Thomas R Machnitzki (thomas@machnitzki.com), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hobbs
summary: Hobbs State Park – Conservation Area (formerly known as Beaver Lake State Park and Hobbs State Management Area) is a 12,056-acre (4,879 ha) Arkansas state park in Benton, Carroll, and Madison Counties, Arkansas in the United States. The park was bought in 1979 through a huge financial effort from Northwest Arkansas banks. Hobbs State Park – Conservation Area is located almost entirely in the Springfield Plateau subdivision of the Ozark Plateau.

image.credit: Doug Wertman from Rogers, AR, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jacksonport
summary: Jacksonport State Park is a 164.7-acre (66.7 ha) Arkansas state park in Jackson County, Arkansas in the United States. The park contains the 1872 Jacksonport courthouse which served as the home of county government from 1872-1892. Furnished with regional items of historical significance, tours of the courthouse are available.

name: Jenkins Ferry
summary: The Jenkins' Ferry Battleground State Park, also known as the Jenkins' Ferry Battlefield, is a battlefield in Grant County, Arkansas. The Arkansas state park commemorates the Battle of Jenkins' Ferry fought on Saturday, April 30, 1864, during the Red River campaign of the American Civil War. First established as a masonic park in the early 20th century, the 40-acre historic site was donated to the state of Arkansas in 1961.

name: Lake Catherine
summary: Lake Catherine State Park is a 2,180-acre (880 ha) public recreation area located on the south shore of Lake Catherine, eight miles (13 km) southeast of Hot Springs, Arkansas. The park was built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Three stone-and-wood cabins, a former concessions building, and a bridge constructed in the Corps' rustic architecture style are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Lake Charles
summary: Lake Charles State Park is a 140-acre (57 ha) Arkansas state park in Lawrence County, Arkansas in the United States. Situated in The Ozarks along the Black River, the park features the 645-acre (261 ha) artificial Lake Charles. The lake is a result of a partnership of four agencies to construct a multipurpose lake just north of Shirey Bay Rainey Brake Wildlife Management Area in an effort to control flooding and preserve the watershed.

name: Lake Chicot
summary: Lake Chicot State Park is a 211.6 acres (85.6 ha) Arkansas state park in Chicot County, Arkansas within the Arkansas Delta. The park is located along Lake Chicot, Arkansas, a 22 miles (35 km) oxbow lake that was formerly the main channel of the Mississippi River. The lake, formerly a polluted eyesore for the area, has been restored to its current condition through the cooperation of many agencies to return its natural, cultural and recreational value.

image.credit: Jeff Noble Camera location 33° 18′ 02.4″ N, 91° 16′ 39″ W View this and other nearby images on: OpenStreetMap 33.300667; -91.277500, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Dardanelle
summary: Lake Dardanelle State Park is located on two sites on the lake, one in Russellville, Arkansas and one in Dardanelle, Arkansas, on the 34,300-acre Lake Dardanelle. Both sites include picnic facilities, boat ramps, pavilions, playgrounds and dump stations. The Russellville Area site features a 10,257 square feet (952.9 m2) visitor center with six aquariums, natural and cultural history displays, classrooms and a gift shop.

image.credit: National Trails Office ( US National Park Service ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Fort Smith
summary: Lake Fort Smith State Park is a 260-acre (110 ha) Arkansas state park in Crawford County, Arkansas in the United States. Originally a Fort Smith city park in the 1930s and later the Works Progress Administration–built Mountainburg Recreational Facility, the lake nestled in the Boston Mountains was adopted into the state park system by the Arkansas Department of Parks and Tourism in 1967. Lake Fort Smith State Park was closed in 2002 to make way for a larger dam and spillway.

image.credit: Doug Wertman from Rogers, AR, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Frierson
summary: Lake Frierson State Park is a 114-acre (46 ha) Arkansas state park on Crowley's Ridge in Greene County, eastern Arkansas. Containing a 335 acres (136 ha) reservoir built by the Soil Conservation Service, the park entered the system in 1975. The park skirts the Crowley's Ridge formation and offers fishing as well as hiking, camping, kayaking, and a visitor center.

image.credit: Thomas R Machnitzki (thomas@machnitzki.com), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Ouachita
summary: Lake Ouachita State Park is a 360-acre (150 ha) public recreation area located ten miles (16 km) northwest of Hot Springs, on the eastern side of Lake Ouachita, which at 40,000 acres (16,000 ha) is the largest man-made lake located entirely within the state of Arkansas. In addition to its recreational offerings, the park preserves the site of the historic Three Sisters springs which were once touted for the curative properties of their mineral waters.

image.credit: Tiffani Sineath from Shreveport, LA, USA, upload by Herrick, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Lake Poinsett
summary: Lake Poinsett State Park is a 132-acre (53 ha) Arkansas state park on Crowley's Ridge in Poinsett County, Arkansas in the United States. The park was formed after the damming of Distress Creek to create a recreational lake in the county in 1960. The park is located along the western bank of the lake and features camping, fishing, picnicking and boat rentals.

image.credit: Thomas R Machnitzki (thomas@machnitzki.com), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Logoly
summary: Logoly State Park is a unit of the Arkansas state parks system located in the Gulf Coastal Plain, 6 miles (10 km) north of Magnolia, 0.75 miles (1.2 km) east of McNeil, off U.S. Route 79 on Logoly Road (County Road 47) in southwestern Arkansas in the United States. The 368-acre (1.49 km2) park surrounds an area of mineral springs that have been known for over a century.

image.credit: Robert Nunnally from Allen, TX, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mammoth Spring
summary: Mammoth Spring State Park is a 62.5-acre (25.3 ha) Arkansas state park in Fulton County, Arkansas in the United States. The park is located surrounding National Natural Landmark of the same name to provide recreation and interpretation for visitors. The park offers fishing, boating and hiking in addition to an Arkansas Welcome Center and restored 1886 Kansas City, Fort Scott and Memphis Railroad (later the St.

name: Marks' Mills
summary: Marks' Mills Battleground State Park is an Arkansas State Park located at the junction of Arkansas Highway 8 and Arkansas Highway 97, north of New Edinburg, Arkansas. It preserves a portion of the battlefield of the Battle of Marks' Mills fought on April 25, 1864, in the Trans-Mississippi Theater of American Civil War. The battle was part of the Camden Expedition.

name: Millwood
summary: Millwood State Park is a public recreation area known for its fishing and wildlife habitats located along the southern side of 29,500-acre (11,900 ha) Millwood Lake, nine miles (14 km) east of Ashdown in Little River County, Arkansas.

name: Moro Bay
summary: Moro Bay State Park is a public recreation area known for its fishing and water recreation at the convergence of Raymond Lake, Moro Bay, and the Ouachita River in Bradley County. The historic towboat and barge used as a ferry across the Ouachita River, Moro Bay ferry, is preserved at the park and listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Mount Nebo
summary: Mount Nebo is a mountain Located near Dardanelle, Arkansas. It has an elevation of 1,350 feet (410 m) above the mountain valleys of west-central Arkansas to an elevation of about 1,755 feet (535 m) above sea level, Mount Nebo has views of 34,000 acres (140 km2) Lake Dardanelle, the Arkansas River and the surrounding mountain ridges. Atop this biblically named plateau is Mount Nebo State Park.

image.credit: Photolitherland ( talk )Chris Litherland, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Parkin Archeological
summary: Parkin Archeological State Park, also known as Parkin Indian Mound, is an archeological site and state park in Parkin, Cross County, Arkansas. Around 1350–1650 CE an aboriginal palisaded village existed at the site, at the confluence of the St. Francis and Tyronza rivers.

name: Pinnacle Mountain
summary: Pinnacle Mountain State Park is a 2,356-acre state park located in Pulaski County, Arkansas just outside of Little Rock. The main attraction is Pinnacle Mountain, an iconic landmark surrounded by the bottomlands of the Big Maumelle and Little Maumelle rivers.

name: Poison Springs
summary: Poison Springs Battleground State Park is an Arkansas state park located southeast of Bluff City. It commemorates the Battle of Poison Spring in the American Civil War, which was part of the 1864 Camden Expedition, an element of a Union Army initiative to gain control of Shreveport, Louisiana, and get a foothold in Texas. In the battle, which was fought on April 18, 1864, Confederates and Choctaw Indians attacked and overcame a supply wagon train of Union soldiers.

image.credit: National Park Service (photos in this publication are NPS unless specifically credited, which this one is not), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Village Creek
summary: Village Creek State Park is a 6,909-acre (2,796 ha) Arkansas state park in Cross and St. Francis counties, Arkansas in the United States. The park was formed as a result of a study commissioned by the Arkansas General Assembly to form a large park in east Arkansas.

image.credit: Thomas R Machnitzki, via Wikimedia Commons

name: White Oak Lake
summary: White Oak Lake State Park is a state park in the southwest of the U.S. state of Arkansas, a few miles from Bluff City. The reservoir sits surrounded by tall pine trees, giving it a rich, wooded beauty. The state park offers camping facilities, hiking and mountain biking trails, boat and bicycle rentals, as well as playground facilities.

image.credit: Robert Nunnally from Allen, TX, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Withrow Springs
summary: Withrow Springs State Park is a 786-acre (318 ha) public recreation area with campgrounds and hiking trails located five miles (8.0 km) north of Huntsville, Arkansas, that serves as a put-in for float trips on War Eagle Creek.

name: Cattail Cove
summary: Cattail Cove State Park is a state park of Arizona, United States, on the shore of Lake Havasu. The park is located on Arizona State Route 95 in far southern Mohave County, about 19 miles (31 km) from Lake Havasu City and 8 miles (13 km) from Parker Strip. The park is public land managed by the Arizona State Parks, and available to the public for recreational purposes.

image.credit: Homer Edward Price, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Dead Horse Ranch
summary: Dead Horse Ranch State Park is a state park of Arizona, United States, on the Verde River in an area known as the Verde River Greenway. Located at approximately 3,300 feet (1,000 m) elevation, Dead Horse Ranch State Park covers 423 acres (1.71 km2) of land with 10 miles (16 km) of hiking trails, 150 campground sites and several picnic areas, along with 23 group camping sites. It also offers trailhead access to the Dead Horse Trail System, located on adjacent Coconino National Forest land.

name: Fort Verde
summary: Fort Verde State Historic Park in the town of Camp Verde, Arizona is a small park that attempts to preserve parts of the Apache Wars-era fort as it appeared in the 1880s. The park was established in 1970 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places a year later.

image.credit: The original uploader was Elf at English Wikipedia ., via Wikimedia Commons

name: Jerome
summary: Jerome State Historic Park is a state park of Arizona, United States, featuring the Douglas Mansion, built in 1916 by a family of influential mining entrepreneurs in Jerome, Arizona, a mining region in the northeast of the Black Hills, east Yavapai County. A museum is located in the old Douglas Mansion. Jerome State Historic Park reopened on October 14, 2010, after being closed since February 27, 2009, because of budget cuts and the need to repair the historic mansion.

name: Lake Havasu
summary: Lake Havasu State Park is a public recreation area located on Lake Havasu in Mohave County, Arizona, United States. The state park provides outdoor recreation opportunities such as camping, boating, and fishing. The Arroyo-Camino Interpretive Garden displays local desert flora.

name: McFarland
summary: McFarland State Historic Park is a historic park located in downtown Florence, Arizona on the corner of Main and Ruggles streets. The park consists of a preserved courthouse and other buildings dating to the Arizona Territory period. The original structure was built in 1878 with the addition of a jail in 1882 and the courthouse in 1891.

image.credit: Tony the Marine ( talk ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Patagonia Lake
summary: Patagonia Lake State Park is a state park of Arizona, United States, on State Route 82, 7 miles (11 km) south of Patagonia, Arizona, containing Patagonia Lake. The 2.5-mile-long (4.0 km), 250-acre (100 ha) lake is a popular southern Arizona site for fishing, camping, boat rental, picnicking, hiking, and birding. Located inside the park is the recently established Sonoita Creek State Natural Area, Arizona's first major state natural area.

image.credit: Photo by Matthew A. Lynn,, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Picacho Peak
summary: Picacho Peak State Park is a state park surrounding Picacho Peak in Picacho, Arizona. The park is located between Casa Grande and Tucson near Interstate 10 in Pinal County. Its centerpiece spire is visible from downtown Tucson, a distance of 45 miles (72 km).

name: Red Rock
summary: Red Rock State Park is a 286-acre (116 ha) state park of Arizona, United States, featuring a red sandstone canyon five miles (8.0 km) southwest the city of Sedona. The main mission of this day-use park is the preservation of the riparian habitat along Oak Creek. Red Rock State Park serves as an environmental education facility for the public and for school or private groups, and provides limited passive recreational opportunities.

image.credit: Wendy from Pennsylvania, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Riordan Mansion
summary: Riordan Mansion State Historic Park is a historic site in Flagstaff, Arizona, bordering Northern Arizona University, that preserves the duplex mansion of lumber barons Timothy and Michael Riordan.

name: Roper Lake
summary: Roper Lake State Park is a public recreation area of Arizona, United States, surrounding 32-acre (13 ha) Roper Lake. It is surrounded by the sky island Pinaleño Mountains range, which include Mount Graham. The state park is located off U.S.

name: Tombstone Courthouse
summary: Tombstone Courthouse State Historic Park is a state park of Arizona in the United States. Located in Tombstone, the park preserves the original Cochise County courthouse. The two-story building, constructed in 1882 in the Victorian style, is laid out in the shape of a cross and once contained various county offices, including those of the sheriff, recorder, treasurer, and the Board of Supervisors as well as courtrooms and a jail.

image.credit: Photo by Matthew A. Lynn,, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tubac Presidio
summary: Tubac Presidio State Historic Park, located in Tubac, Arizona, United States, preserves the ruins of the Presidio San Ignacio de Tubac and various other buildings, thereby presenting a timeline of European settlement in this Southern Arizona town. The park contains a museum, a number of historic sites, an underground archeology exhibit displaying the excavated foundations of the Tubac Presidio, and a picnic area. Various cultural events are held on-site throughout the year including Anza Days in October.

name: Ahjumawi Lava Springs
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Ahjumawi Lava Springs State Park is a state park of California in the United States. It is located in remote northeastern Shasta County and is only accessible to the public by boat. The park is 4 miles (6.4 km) in length and no more than 1 mile (1.6 km) wide, and has over 13 miles (21 km) of shoreline.

name: Andrew Molera
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Andrew Molera State Park is a 7.5-square-mile (19-square-kilometer), relatively undeveloped state park on the Big Sur coast of California, United States, preserving land as requested by former owner Frances Molera. Situated at the mouth of the Big Sur River, the property was part of the Rancho El Sur land grant, and later owned by Californio pioneer John Bautista Rogers Cooper and his descendants. Cooper's grandchildren Andrew and Frances Molera inherited the property from their mother in 1918.

name: Angel Island
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Angel Island (Spanish: Isla de los Ángeles) is an island in San Francisco Bay. The entire island is included within Angel Island State Park, administered by California State Parks. The island, a California Historical Landmark, has been used for a variety of purposes, including seasonal hunting and gathering by Indigenous peoples, water and timber supply for European ships, ranching by Mexicans, United States military installations, a United States Public Health Service Quarantine Station, and a U.S.

name: Annadel
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Trione-Annadel State Park is a California state park in the United States. It is situated at the northern edge of Sonoma Valley and is adjacent to Spring Lake Regional Park in Santa Rosa. It offers many recreational activities within its 5,092-acre (2,061 ha) property.

image.credit: Brian Michelsen from Santa Rosa, California, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Arthur B. Ripley Desert Woodland
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Arthur B. Ripley Desert Woodland State Park is a state park in the western Antelope Valley in Southern California. The park protects mature stands of Joshua trees (Yucca brevifolia) and California juniper trees (Juniperus californica) in their western Mojave Desert habitat.

name: Asilomar
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Asilomar State Beach, officially Asilomar State Beach and Conference Grounds State Park, is a state park unit of California, United States. It provides public access to rocky coast and dune habitat on the Monterey Peninsula. The property includes the Asilomar Conference Grounds, a conference center built by the YWCA in 1913 that is now a National Historic Landmark.

image.credit: Joyce Cory on Flickr as docentjoyce from Los Osos, u.s.a., via Wikimedia Commons

name: Año Nuevo
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Año Nuevo State Park is a state park of California, United States, encompassing Año Nuevo Island and Año Nuevo Point, which are known for their pinniped rookeries. Located in San Mateo County, the low, rocky, windswept point juts out into the Pacific Ocean about 55 miles (89 km) south of San Francisco and the Golden Gate. Año Nuevo State Natural Reserve, formerly a separate unit of the California state park system, was merged into Año Nuevo State Park in October 2008.

image.credit: Mecil ( talk ) ( Uploads ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bean Hollow
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Bean Hollow State Beach is a beach in the state park system of California, United States. It is located in San Mateo County near Pescadero. The beach offers fishing, picnicking and beachcombing.

image.credit: Doug Dolde aka Doug Dolde at en.wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bidwell-Sacramento River
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Bidwell–Sacramento River State Park is a state park of California, United States, preserving riparian habitat on the Sacramento River and its tributary Big Chico Creek. The park is located on the border of Butte County and Glenn County. Common activities include fishing for salmon, steelhead and shad; and floating the river on inner tubes, canoes or kayaks.

image.credit: Sharon Hahn Darlin, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bolsa Chica
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Bolsa Chica State Beach is a public ocean beach in Orange County, California, United States. It is surrounded entirely by the city of Huntington Beach to the north and east, and to the northwest by the Huntington Beach community of Sunset Beach and the Pacific Ocean to the west. The beach extends 3 miles (5 km) from Warner Avenue in Sunset Beach south to Seapoint Avenue, where the Huntington City Beach begins.

name: Border Field
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Border Field State Park is a state park of California, United States, containing beach and coastal habitat on the Mexico–United States border. The park is within the city limits of Imperial Beach in San Diego County, next to the suburb of Playas de Tijuana in Mexico. It contains the southernmost point in the state of California.

image.credit: Tony Webster from Portland, Oregon, United States, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bothe-Napa Valley
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Bothe-Napa Valley State Park is a state park of California in the United States. Located in the Napa Valley, it contains the farthest inland coast redwoods in a California state park. The 1,991-acre (806 ha) park was established in 1960.

name: Burleigh H. Murray Ranch
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Burleigh H. Murray Ranch is a property in the state park system of California in the United States. It is a valley ranch located in San Mateo County inland from Half Moon Bay.

name: Burton Creek
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Burton Creek State Park is a state park in the U.S. state of California, located in Placer County near Truckee. Situated on the outskirts of Tahoe City, the park offers 6 miles (9.7 km) of unpaved roadway for hiking and cross-country skiing. The 1,890-acre (760 ha) park was established in 1976.

name: Butano
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Butano State Park is a state park in the U.S. state of California, showcasing the secluded redwood-filled canyon of Little Butano Creek, a tributary of Butano Creek in the Pescadero Creek watershed. Located in San Mateo County near Pescadero, the 4,728-acre (1,913 ha) park was established in 1956.

name: Calaveras Big Trees
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Calaveras Big Trees State Park is a state park of California, United States, preserving two groves of giant sequoia trees. Located four miles (6.4 km) northeast of Arnold in the middle elevations of the Sierra Nevada, it has been a major tourist attraction since 1852, when the existence of the trees was first widely reported. Two famous exhibition trees, the Discovery Tree and the Mother of the Forest, were felled for display.

name: Cardiff
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Cardiff State Beach is a California State Beach in San Diego County, California, United States. Popular activities include swimming, surfing, and beachcombing. Just next to Cardiff State Beach is San Elijo State Beach, which has a state-run campground.

name: Carlsbad
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Carlsbad State Beach is a protected beach in the state park system of California, United States, located in Carlsbad. It is a San Diego County beach with coastal bluffs. Popular activities include swimming, surfing and bodyboarding several nearby breaks, scuba diving, fishing, and beachcombing.

name: Carmel River
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Carmel River State Beach is a state park unit at the mouth of Carmel Valley, California, United States, featuring a 1-mile-long (1.6 km) protected beach with a lagoon formed by the Carmel River. The lagoon attracts many migratory birds. The state beach includes Mara Beach and Monastery Beach, (also called San Jose Creek Beach) which is popular with scuba divers.

name: Carpinteria
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Carpinteria State Beach is a protected beach in the state park system of California, in Santa Barbara County, Southern California.

name: Caspar Headlands
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Caspar Headlands State Beach is a protected beach in the state park system of California, United States. It is located in Northern California in Mendocino County near the village of Caspar. The 75-acre (30 ha) park was established in 1972.

name: Castle Crags
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Castle Crags is a dramatic and well-known rock formation in Northern California. Elevations range from 2,000 feet (610 m) along the Sacramento River near the base of the crags, to over 6,500 feet (2,000 m) at the summit of the tallest crag. Located just west of Interstate 5, between the towns of Castella and Dunsmuir, Castle Crags is today a popular tourist stop along the highway.

name: Castle Rock
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Castle Rock State Park is a 5,242-acre (2,121 ha) state park of California, United States, located along the crest of the Santa Cruz Mountains and almost entirely in Santa Cruz County, with parts extending into Santa Clara County and San Mateo County. It embraces coast redwood, Douglas fir, and madrone forest, most of which has been left in its wild, natural state. Steep canyons are sprinkled with unusual rock formations that are a popular rock climbing area.

name: Caswell Memorial
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Caswell Memorial State Park is a state park of California, United States, preserving a riparian forest along the Stanislaus River. It is located in southern San Joaquin County southwest of the town of Ripon. Riparian Oak Woodland, located in this park, is threatened and the park is trying to protect it.

name: Cayucos
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Cayucos State Beach is a protected beach in the state park system of California, United States. It is located in Cayucos, San Luis Obispo County. The sandy beach environment supports uses of swimming and surfing.

name: China Camp
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: China Camp State Park is a state park in Marin County, California, surrounding a historic Chinese American shrimp-fishing village and a salt marsh. The park is located in San Rafael, California, on the shore of San Pablo Bay. It is known for its hiking and mountain biking trails, scenic views, and open spaces.

name: Chino Hills
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Chino Hills State Park is a state park of California, in the United States. It is located in the Chino Hills, foothills of the Santa Ana Mountains. It is a critical link in the Chino–Puente Hills wildlife corridor, and a major botanical habitat reserve for resident and migrating wildlife.

name: Clear Lake
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Clear Lake State Park is a state park of California, United States, on Clear Lake. The park is popular for water recreation. Amenities include 149 developed campsites spread across four campground areas, two group campsites, a swimming beach with showers, a boat launch, and a marina.

name: Crystal Cove
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Crystal Cove State Park is a state park of California, United States, encompassing 3.2 miles (5.1 km) of Pacific coastline, inland chaparral canyons, and the Crystal Cove Historic District of beach houses. The park is located partially in Newport Beach and partially in an unincorporated area of Orange County, and is part of the larger South Coast Wilderness area. Crystal Cove is a stretch of coastal cliffs and a beachfront cove situated between the Pacific Coast Highway and the Pacific Ocean, southeast of Newport Beach and northwest of Laguna Beach.

image.credit: Don Ramey Logan, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Cuyamaca Rancho
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Cuyamaca Rancho State Park is a state park in inland San Diego County, California, United States, located 40 miles (64 km) east of the metropolitan area of San Diego. The park is situated near the southernmost reaches of the Cleveland National Forest, as well as the Cuyamaca and Laguna Mountains of the Peninsular Ranges. The park's 26,000 acres (11,000 ha) of land features pine, fir, and oak forests, interspersed with meadows, creeks and streams that exist due to the relatively high elevation of the area when compared to its surroundings.

name: D.L. Bliss
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: D. L. Bliss State Park is a state park of California in the United States.

name: Del Norte Coast Redwoods
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Del Norte Coast Redwoods State Park is a state park of California, United States, and a component of the Redwood National and State Parks. The park is about half old-growth forest of coast redwoods and includes 8 miles (13 km) of wild Pacific coastline. The park was significantly expanded in 2002 with the 39 mi2 (100 km2) Mill Creek Addition.

name: Doheny
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Doheny State Beach (known colloquially as Doho) is known as the first state beach in the California state park system. Located on the Pacific Ocean in the city of Dana Point, the beach is adjacent to several surf spots and scenic beaches including Salt Creek Beach, Baby Beach, and Capistrano Beach. Along with its neighbors, Doheny beach is a popular surf spot located at the mouth of San Juan Creek, which flows from the Santa Ana Mountains southwest to the beach, where it forms a fresh-water lagoon.

name: Donner Memorial
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Donner Memorial State Park is a California State Park, located at the town of Truckee, California, United States. The park preserves a portion of the Donner Camp site, where members of the ill-fated Donner Party were trapped just short of Donner Pass by weather during the winter of 1846–1847. Caught without shelter or adequate supplies, members of the group resorted to cannibalism to survive.

name: Ed Z'Berg Sugar Pine Point
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation

name: El Capitán
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: El Capitán State Beach is a protected beach in the state park system of California. The most easterly of three state parks along the Gaviota Coast, it is located about 20 miles (32 km) west of downtown Santa Barbara, in Santa Barbara County. The beach is named for José Francisco Ortega, who retired from the Spanish Army in 1795 with the rank of captain and received the Rancho Nuestra Señora del Refugio as a land grant.

name: Emma Wood
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Emma Wood State Beach is a California State Beach in Ventura, California. It is located on the Santa Barbara Channel on the west side of the Ventura River estuary and south of the railroad tracks of the Coast Line and the US Highway 101 freeway. The beach is named after Emma Grubb Wood who once owned the 8,000 acres (3,237 ha) Taylor Ranch.

name: Estero Bluffs
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Estero Bluffs State Park is a state park of California, United States, on Estero Bay. The park protects a grassland-dominated marine terrace that slopes from California State Route 1 to the Pacific Ocean. The property is crossed by San Geronimo and Villa Creeks and is just north of the town of Cayucos.

image.credit: Mike Baird from Morro Bay, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Fort Ord Dunes
managedBy: California Department of Parks and Recreation
summary: Fort Ord Dunes State Park is a state park in California, United States, along 4 miles (6.4 km) of coastline on Monterey Bay and created from part of the closed Fort Ord. The park includes a boardwalk, a path to the beach, a 4-mile (6.4 km) road for walking and biking, and interpretive exhibits describing its former use as a military training area.
